Candid Chat Agent.tagline: An agentic chat surface for the public sector, and the work of deciding what it should look like while it is thinking.
Candid Chat Agent.cover: Cover — Ask Candid at rest, and a prompt going in

meta.v: Front-end lead · client-side chat architecture, UI states

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Solving problems for the public sector
paras: Candid serves the public sector. The people who open this are after the same two things — who might fund them, and which RFPs are open — and the agent’s job was to go and find both rather than hand back another search page.
I led the front end: architecting how the chat behaved on the client, and working with design to turn the workflows running underneath it into something a person could read while they ran.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Discovering chat states
blocks.note: A user journey is only ambiguous until the states are written down.
paras: The initial states of the chat app felt empty and confusing due and I recognized it was due to a lack of chat bar states. An open text box promises anything, which is another way of saying it explains nothing. The design problem was never the conversation — it was the moment before it, during, and after the conversation: what the bar looks like before you have typed, while it submits, while an answer is still arriving, and when the agent is busy doing something other than talking.

So I chose to enumerate them. Every state the surface could be in got named and given a treatment, and the chat bar became one component that had to hold all of them without becoming a different thing in each.

items.caption: The chat bar, from empty to submitted
Walking the chat surface in early development

items.title: Show the answer forming
items.body: A model takes seconds to answer. Something has to happen in those seconds, and there are only two honest options: a loading state, or the answer itself arriving in pieces.

chose.v: Streaming. Tokens render as they arrive, so the wait is spent reading rather than watching a spinner.

passed.v: Holding the response back and revealing it complete — steadier to build, but every question costs the same silent pause.

items.call: The cost is real: a half-formed answer can read as a wrong one before it finishes. That is an argument for designing the streaming state carefully, not for hiding it. This added a lot of technical collaboration with the data team to define the tool call structure for the streaming states.

blocks.label: Payoff
blocks.title: In use
paras: The hard part was not the streaming — it was keeping the page still while it happened. Content grows underneath the reader, and a surface that reflows or jumps each time a token lands is harder to read than the spinner would have been.

items.caption: So we have to build around the variability and define what we can while data is settling

blocks.label: REFLECTION
blocks.title: Continue Building
paras: Development continues and products are ever evolving using new AI tools.One thing I'd love to think further through next is the longer term product vision. This product opened up a lot of opportunity to upgrade the users workflow further and spending the time to think through the longer term vision should allow for quicker integration between distinct systems.

index.summary: Agentic chat experience that exposes automatic workflows for the public sector.

Max's Lab.tagline: A 3D world built to gamify a product release, and the architecture that let marketing keep building on it afterwards.
Max's Lab.cover: Cover — 8s loop of the world at first load, camera settling

meta.v: Lead front end · architecture, asset pipeline, controls

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: How do you gamify a product release?
paras: That was the brief, and it arrived as a question rather than a design. Nobody knew what the answer looked like, so the project opened with a round of fast prototyping alongside design — building the options quickly enough that we could look at them instead of argue about them.
A navigable 3D world won. Everything after that was the work of making one run properly on the web, which is mostly a series of decisions about what the assets are allowed to cost.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Prototyping in the open
paras: The explorations lived in a Storybook rather than in somebody’s branch. Camera controls, loaders, color and polygon studies, pathfinding — each one a story with its own controls, so design could open any of them and change the parameters without booking an engineer.

The pathfinding studies are the ones worth showing: a demo map, a nav mesh you can switch on to see what the movement is actually solving, and the same level under first-person, third-person and keyboard cameras.

items.caption: Navigation pathfinding — nav mesh on, first-person keyboard camera

items.title: Control options, not one control scheme
items.body: A 3D world on the web is reached from a phone, a trackpad and a keyboard, and each of those wants something different. The tempting move is to tune one scheme until it is good enough everywhere.

chose.v: Several schemes, offered together — tap to move, drag to rotate, and a d-pad you hold to steer — so the world was reachable however somebody arrived at it.

passed.v: A single scheme, tuned for the input we expected most. Cheaper to build and cheaper to explain.

items.call: Controls are the part of a 3D experience that decides who can use it at all. Treating them as an accessibility question rather than a taste question is what made the room reachable for the whole audience.

items.title: Polygon budgets set with design, during
items.body: Web 3D fails late. Assets get made, the scene gets assembled, and the performance problem shows up when there is no time left to change what caused it.

chose.v: Budgets agreed with design while the assets were still being built — redefining GLTF polygon counts and texture sizes as part of the modelling conversation, not after it.

passed.v: Building for fidelity and optimising at the end, which is the normal way and puts the whole cost on the last week.

items.call: It made the pipeline the deliverable rather than the scene. That is also why there was something left to build on.

items.title: Exploration Controls
items.body: When a user is explore a 3D world movement has to feel fun and engaging, otherwise the entire moment's foundation could taint the overall experience.

chose.v: Navigation map based exploration with a deliverable navigation bounding the player to a specified space.

passed.v: Physics based exploration where users can experience items pushing against each other and realistic gravity.

items.call: Nav mesh was chosen for device accessibility as we had the data to see what kinds of devices are users are on. A considerable amount of users could potentially see a performance hit if we went with the physics approach.

items.k: Increase in user interactions and sessions duration

items.note: first pre-order in the company's history

blocks.label: Outcome
blocks.title: It earned a second chapter
paras: The room was built composably enough that marketing bought a part two on it — a second story told in the same world, to sell more product through the same lens. That is the outcome I would point at: not that the experience shipped, but that the thing underneath it was worth extending.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: Improving Further
paras: If I had the ability to keep working on this project I'd add alot more device telemetry such as temp, frames, etc to get more experience performance data on their range of devices.I'd also use a lot of my new 3D skills to provide more help on the modeling and styling side of this experience.

index.summary: An explorable 3D world built to gamify a product release.

Moodie.tagline: An infinite discovery canvas for collecting and exploring visual inspiration.
Moodie.cover: Cover — canvas pan and zoom, boards resolving

meta.v: Solo, with a handful of very patient testers

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it exists
paras: My own reference collection had become four thousand screenshots in a folder. Every tool I tried made me file things, and filing is the step where collecting dies.
Moodie has no folders. Everything lands on one infinite canvas, and proximity is the only organising principle.
blocks.pull: Filing is the step where collecting dies.

blocks.label: Context
blocks.title: Why it matters
paras: It is the piece I use to test how far interaction can carry structure. If spatial memory can replace a taxonomy for four thousand items, that is worth knowing.

blocks.label: Process
blocks.title: Process assets
blocks.note: Mostly performance work disguised as interaction work.

items.caption: Tile virtualization at four zoom levels
Drop → thumbnail → placed, in one gesture

items.title: No search
items.body: The obvious feature. I have not built it, on purpose, for a year.

chose.v: Zoom-to-find. Getting somewhere is always a movement, never a query.

passed.v: Text search over tags and OCR.

items.call: Search would let me stop designing the canvas. Every time I have wanted it, the real problem was that zoom was too slow — and that was fixable.

items.title: Local-first with no account
items.body: No sync means no server, no auth, no privacy policy, and no access from a second machine.

chose.v: IndexedDB, with export to a single file.

items.call: The export file is the sync story until someone other than me needs it.

blocks.label: Reflection
blocks.title: Where it stands
paras: It holds my whole reference library and I have not opened the old folder in months, which is the only success metric I set.
The next problem is sharing a region without sharing the canvas. That probably requires the account I have been avoiding.

index.summary: An infinite discovery canvas for collecting and exploring visual inspiration.
